groups.name: Fundamentals and cryptography
groups.reason: Ch 1 gives the vocabulary used in every later chapter (CIA, threat, vulnerability, attack, countermeasure). Ch 2 supplies hashes, signatures and certificates that Ch 3, 4 and 8 reuse (Ch 2 S26 lists passwords and intrusion detection as hash uses).

groups.name: Authentication and access control
groups.reason: The lecturer's own summary slide (CH4 S3) calls identification and authentication the first fine-grained service and access control the second.

groups.name: Database and data centre security
groups.reason: Uses Ch 4 (DAC, RBAC, GRANT/REVOKE) and introduces SQL injection, which Ch 11 reuses (CH11 S15).

groups.name: Malware and denial of service
groups.reason: Bots and zombies (Ch 6 S43–44) are the machines behind DDoS (Ch 7 S12–13).

groups.name: Intrusion detection, firewalls and IPS
groups.reason: IPS is "an extension of an IDS" (CH9 S29), and Snort appears in both. Together they cover how to detect and block the attacks of Ch 6–7.

groups.name: Buffer overflow and software security
groups.reason: Ch 11 builds on Ch 10 (input size, numeric validation) and Ch 5 (injection).

groups.name: Cloud and IoT
groups.reason: Most self-contained chapter. It touches Ch 4 only through identity and access management (Table 13.2).

jointFormat.intro: Use this for every session. The purpose is understanding, not Kyle lecturing. David explains first on any topic he has studied.

parts.short: 12 min: take turns, no notes, each explains two concepts and the other adds what is missing
10 min: both attempt the same example separately, then compare
5 min: each asks two "why", "what if", "compare", "limit" or "how could this be asked" questions

recoveryRules: The practice day (Fri 20) is never used to recover lost time.

workspace.tierNote: Verified = taken from the course files (slide counts, slide numbers, practicals). Estimate = my planning guess (hours, pace, complexity). Assumption = something I had to assume about you or about the material. Section 4 keeps these apart. MUST/SHOULD/COULD describe time-allocation priorities, never examination likelihood or exclusions; all prescribed slides remain examinable.

sessions.title: Ch 1 and Ch 2

tasks.text: Ch 1: S4–7 (definition, CIA, impact levels), S10–15 (terminology, assets, vulnerabilities, threats, attacks, countermeasures), S21–22 (Table 1.3, passive vs active attacks), S34 (learn the names of the 13 design principles), S35–36 (attack surfaces). Example: fill a CIA table with Low/Moderate/High and a reason for one system you choose.

Ch 2: S3–8 (symmetric encryption and attacks), S9–13 (DES, 3DES, AES; Tables 2.1 and 2.2), S17 (block vs stream), S18–26 (message authentication, MAC, hash properties), S27–35 (public-key encryption), S36–38 (digital signatures), and Practical 1 (S46–47): do one complete double columnar transposition, decrypting with the second key first. The ST1 Q4 marked solution is a worked example: attempt first, then compare.
Ch 2: S14–16, S22–24 (figures), S39–44 (certificates, digital envelopes, random numbers, stored-data encryption), a second timed transposition run.
Ch 1: S8–9 (ten challenges), S16–19 (Table 1.2, open the images), S23–33 (17 FIPS families).

sessions.outcome: can explain CIA and the threat vocabulary; can compare symmetric, public-key, hash, MAC and signature; can run the transposition.

sessions.title: J5: Main joint day (adaptive block plan)

tasks.text: Teach-back + an appropriate technical example, ideally malware/DoS/IDS — David: Explain only topics both have prepared; otherwise do a clearly labelled introductory overview
Ch 9–11 applications and Ch 13 model comparisons, adapted to progress — David: Explain-back only for studied content; otherwise identify outstanding first-pass topics

sessions.notes:
Do not lock this schedule until the evening of 18 November. Use the actual progress tracker to choose between the following options. An unstudied topic cannot become "learned" merely because Kyle explained it for ten minutes.
Full day: T1 independent 2 h · T2 joint 45 min · lunch 45 min · T3 independent 2 h · break 15 min · T4 independent 1 h 15 min · T5 joint 60 min · break 15 min · T6 joint 45 min (Section 9.3).
Adjustment rule 1: If David is ahead of Q9, move the joint content forward accordingly and spend extra time on independent questions, not duplicated teaching.
Adjustment rule 2: If David is at Q6–Q9, shorten the old-chapter T6 block and allocate the joint time to the new topics he has actually prepared; continue first-pass reading independently.
Adjustment rule 3: If David is behind Q6, use Scenario D: a minimum-exposure sweep across remaining chapter headings and their key concepts, with technical drills reserved for selected procedures. Do not mark those chapters as first-pass complete.
Adjustment rule 4: If either student is fatigued, reduce Kyle's SHOULD deepening and shorten T6 first. Preserve the required independent study and critical technical practice wherever feasible; do not extend beyond the ~9 h elapsed template.
Adjustment rule 5: Friday 20 remains practice and revision. If a chapter is still untouched, the practice results and tracker must acknowledge that rather than claiming all content was covered.

sessions.title: Practice and revision only

tasks.text: Active-recall warm-up (Independent): Blank-page recall of each chapter group, about 3 min per chapter, then check against the slides

Technical drills (Independent, timed): Rotate across all major procedure types: transposition, revocation graph, TCP handshake, packet-filter rule evaluation, hex stack trace, 8-bit example and SQLi/XSS. If seven full problems cannot fit, do short representative versions and complete any unfinished types in P5. Track which procedures each person actually attempted
Timed mock (Independent, closed book): 60 marks (1.8 min per mark), all twelve chapters represented, in test-style formats
Targeted repair (Independent): From Section 14: retrieval practice on the chapters that showed gaps, using the slides as the answer key. This is not new learning.

sessions.notes:
No planned first-time chapter learning. The target is productive, not exhausting: 6 h active and about 6 h 50 min elapsed with the specified breaks. Each person attempts everything independently before comparing. Use the semester test only to match the lecturer's format and expectations (matching, tables to copy, select-all picture items, argued short answers, one long procedure, a scenario). Mock questions and a memorandum are not generated yet. Ask Claude to produce two separate files (unseen paper and private answer key) by Thursday evening after the 19 Nov session; do not display solutions while sitting the mock. Questions should sample across all 12 examinable chapters, not just those already covered, and any omissions must be called out.
Block order: P1 → P2 → break 30 min → P3 → break 20 min → P4 (joint, J6) → P5 → P6 (joint, J6).
Coverage check. Map the 60-mark mock against Ch 1–11 and 13: each chapter must appear at least once, although the marks need not be equal. Use P2 to cover practical mechanisms that a short mock cannot test in depth.
Options. If both feel well prepared, replace P3 + P5 with a full 100-mark, 3-hour mock plus 90 min marking. If either is behind (Scenario C or D), run a 40-mark mock on the studied chapters and extend P2. Stop at a sensible hour and sleep.
